The study models a composite-aluminum single-lap bolted joint with a countersunk titanium fastener.
The composite plate is made of HTA/6376 CFRP with a quasi-isotropic stacking sequence.
The aluminum plate is AA7475-T76.
The titanium bolt is Ti–6Al–4VSTA with finger-tight pretension.
The fitting tolerance between bolt and hole is 10–70 μm.
The model uses eight-node brick elements with reduced integration (C3D8R) in Abaqus.
Aluminum and titanium are modeled with elasto-plastic material behavior and isotropic hardening.
The composite material uses the ply-discount method for progressive damage modeling.
Contact is modeled with a Coulomb friction coefficient of 0.2.
Failure criteria are based on Olmedo and Santiuste, Chang and Chang, and Chang and Lessard.
The model is validated against experimental results from Ireman et al.
The experimental maximum load before failure is just below 14 kN.
The study shows that temperature differences significantly affect fastener forces.
Non-linear joint response leads to less conservative load distribution at ultimate failure.
Connector elements represent fasteners in the structural model.
The Building Block Approach is recommended for composite assembly certification.
The model captures damage initiation and development up to failure.
Progressive damage is implemented using the USDFLD subroutine in Abaqus.
The analysis uses automatic time stepping with a maximum load increment of 1% of the total applied load.
The model is terminated when severe convergence difficulties are encountered.
The study evaluates the impact of temperature and non-linear response on hybrid wing structures.
The paper highlights the challenges in modeling hybrid composite-aluminum joints.
The model is used to evaluate local force–displacement responses of several joint configurations.
The study demonstrates the importance of considering non-linear joint behavior in design.
The paper provides a methodology for simulating structures with hybrid CFRP-aluminum joints.
